raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic systolic heart failure syndrome occurring toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause and with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) usually <45% [1–3]. The traditional National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute definition restricted onset to the last gestational month through 5 months postpartum, whereas contemporary European definitions emphasize the peripartum clinical context rather than a rigid time window [1–4]. This distinction matters because similar pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy may present earlier in gestation and appears clinically continuous with classic PPCM [12].

The reported incidence varies widely by geography and ascertainment. Contemporary estimates range from approximately 1 in 1000–4000 live births in high-income settings to much higher rates in regions such as Haiti and parts of Africa [5,8,11,13]. In a North Carolina population-based study, birth prevalence was 1 in 2772 live births, with marked racial disparities and 16.5% 7-year case fatality [11]. Risk factors include African ancestry, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, multifetal pregnancy, older maternal age, multiparity, anemia, and socioeconomic disadvantage [4,9,29,30]. Global registry data show substantial regional heterogeneity in presentation, treatment, recovery, and maternal and neonatal outcomes [9].

Pathogenesis is multifactorial. Current models integrate late-pregnancy hemodynamic stress, genetic susceptibility, vascular dysfunction, oxidative stress, and hormonal-angiogenic imbalance [5,13,14]. A landmark experimental study implicated STAT3 deficiency, cathepsin-D activation, and cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic and proapoptotic fragment [14]. A complementary vascular hypothesis demonstrated that antiangiogenic signaling, particularly soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1), can promote PPCM in susceptible myocardium [15]. Translational IPAC data found higher sFlt1 associated with worse symptoms and adverse events, while relaxin-2 related to early recovery [16]. Recent work has again linked cathepsin-D levels with disease severity [17]. Genetics is increasingly important: truncating variants in cardiomyopathy genes, especially TTN, occur in a meaningful minority and overlap with dilated cardiomyopathy genetics [18,19].

Clinically, PPCM often presents with dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, cough, palpitations, chest discomfort, or cardiogenic shock; these symptoms overlap with normal pregnancy, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pre-eclampsia, and anemia, delaying diagnosis [4,6]. Echocardiography is central, documenting reduced LVEF and assessing LV size, right ventricular function, valvular disease, pulmonary pressures, and intracardiac thrombus [2,3,6]. Natriuretic peptides are useful because normal values argue against heart failure, whereas elevation is not specific [27]. Troponin, inflammatory markers, angiogenic biomarkers, and cardiac magnetic resonance may aid selected cases, but none replace clinical assessment and echocardiography [16,28]. ECG abnormalities and arrhythmias are common enough to warrant vigilance, particularly when LVEF is severely reduced [24,26].

Management requires a cardio-obstetric team, maternal stabilization, fetal assessment when antepartum, and guideline-directed heart failure therapy adapted to pregnancy and lactation [3,6,7]. During pregnancy, diuretics, beta-blockers such as metoprolol, hydralazine-nitrates, and anticoagulation when indicated are commonly used; angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are generally avoided until after delivery [6,7]. Postpartum therapy follows heart failure with reduced ejection fraction principles, considering lactation safety and shared decision-making [3,4,6]. Severe presentations require intensive care, cautious diuresis, vasodilators if blood pressure permits, inotropes or mechanical circulatory support for shock, and early referral to advanced heart failure centers [3,20]. Thromboembolism is a recognized complication, particularly with very low LVEF, LV thrombus, atrial fibrillation, or bromocriptine use; registry data support careful individualized anticoagulation [25]. Wearable defibrillators may bridge the early recovery period in patients with severe LV dysfunction, whereas permanent ICD decisions are usually deferred until recovery potential is clearer [10,24,26].

Bromocriptine, a dopamine agonist that suppresses prolactin, is the main disease-specific therapy studied. A South African pilot trial suggested benefit in acute severe PPCM [21], and a German randomized multicenter study found high recovery and low event rates with short- or longer-course bromocriptine added to standard therapy, although it did not include a placebo arm [20]. Meta-analyses suggest improved LVEF recovery signals but remain limited by small trials, confounding, and regional practice variation; when used, bromocriptine should generally be paired with anticoagulation and lactation counseling [22].

Prognosis depends strongly on baseline LVEF, LV dimensions, right ventricular involvement, race/geography, genetic substrate, and treatment access [8–10,18]. In IPAC, most women improved, but recovery was less likely with LVEF <30%, LV dilation, and African ancestry [8]. Subsequent pregnancy is a major counseling issue: persistent LV dysfunction confers high risk and is generally discouraged; even after apparent recovery, relapse can occur, so preconception evaluation, contraception counseling, and close surveillance are essential [23,24]. Future priorities include earlier recognition, equitable access to cardio-obstetric care, validated biomarkers, genotype-informed counseling, and adequately powered randomized trials of targeted therapies [3–5,22].
